newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU mulls enlargement forum to appease outsiders.
newsitem.headline: EU mulls enlargement forum to appease outsiders.

text.p: The European Union, afraid of leaving some countries out in the cold in the bloc's next enlargement, floated the idea on Saturday of an ante-room to keep hopeful countries on track for eventual entry.

Foreign ministers, meeting for an informal chat in the Dutch town of Apeldoorn, asked France and the Dutch EU presidency to come up with more precise plans for Paris' idea of a standing conference on EU enlargement.
"It's something that would be in place to keep the dialogue going with those who would not immediately qualify for enlargement," one EU diplomat said.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said the conference would not amount to a waiting room for frustrated EU hopefuls.
"It will be a genuine conference," he told a news conference.

The idea arose during discussion of one of the EU's biggest long-term foreign policy dilemmas -- whether to open talks with all or just the adequately prepared from a list of 10 eastern countries pinning their hopes on membership of the rich western club.

Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Romania, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have all been promised eventual EU membership, but only a handful are seen as up to scratch at present.
The concern is that countries struggling to distance themselves from their Soviet past are the ones most likely to be left out of NATO and the EU and could end up alientated.

EU diplomats said the conference -- which at the end of the discussion remained a loose concept -- could also offer solace to Turkey, a NATO ally bitterly resentful of being left out of the EU plans while former enemies are being taken on board.

Ankara's EU application has been rejected by the EU on human rights grounds and the EU is under pressure to take a clear stand towards the strategically placed country after a strong snub by centre-rightist EU leaders recently.
"It's important that we have a way of handling Turkey's interests in the EU in a way that's fair, that's objective," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind told a news conference.
He said Turkey should be reassured that it was being treated on an equal footing with other countries who might not be deemed to meet up to EU standards. "We have to be able to
demonstrate to Turkey that she's not being treated to a different set of rules to everyone else," he said.
Meanwhile the EU members remained divided on Saturday about the approach to enlarging the EU eastwards.

While countries like Britain said there was no point in opening entry negotiations with all the candidates, only to let some drop later, countries like Sweden and Denmark are anxious to bring all on track immediately.
EU expansion talks are scheduled to start six months after the end of the EU's ongoing intergovernmental review of its workings, designed to prepare the bloc for the day it has more than 25 members.
Those talks are scheduled to wrap up at the EU's Amsterdam summit in June.
